buckets.title: Work, Energy, Power & Mechanical Energy Conservation

microtopics.title: Work, Energy, Power & Mechanical Energy Conservation
entry_assumptions: **Work-Energy Theorem Generality Invariant**: The net work done on a particle by *all* acting forces (conservative, non-conservative, and external) strictly equals the change in kinetic energy: $W_{\text{net}} = W_{\text{c}} + W_{\text{nc}} + W_{\text{ext}} = \Delta K = \frac{1}{2}m v_f^2 - \frac{1}{2}m v_i^2$. This holds in any inertial frame regardless of force nature.

**Mechanical Energy Conservation Condition Invariant**: Mechanical energy $E_{\text{mech}} = K + U$ is conserved ($\Delta E_{\text{mech}} = 0$) **if and only if** the net work done by all non-conservative and non-potential forces vanishes: $W_{\text{nc}} + W_{\text{ext}} = 0$. Stating $K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f$ in the presence of unmodeled friction or inelastic deformation is a fatal physical error.

**Potential Energy Definition Invariant**: Potential energy is defined exclusively for conservative forces via the line integral: $\Delta U = - W_{\text{c}} = -\int_{\vec{r}_i}^{\vec{r}_f} \vec{F}_{\text{c}} \cdot d\vec{r}$. Potential energy cannot be assigned to dissipative or non-conservative interactions (e.g. kinetic friction).
microtopics.inferential_jump: Work as a scalar path integral of force along displacement: $W = \int \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r} = \int (F_x dx + F_y dy + F_z dz)$. For constant force, $W = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{d} = F d \cos\theta$.

teaching_path.action: Conservation of Mechanical Energy condition: $W_{\text{nc}} = 0 \implies \Delta (K + U) = 0$. In general: $K_i + U_i + W_{\text{nc}} + W_{\text{ext}} = K_f + U_f$.

Energy accounting workflow: (1) Define isolated system boundary, (2) Identify conservative forces and associate potential energy functions ($mgh, \frac{1}{2}kx^2$), (3) Calculate line work of non-conservative forces along actual path, (4) Formulate work-energy equation.
Discrimination between instantaneous power $P = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{v}$ and average power $P_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta W}{\Delta t}$ in variable velocity systems.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Writing $mgh = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$ for a block sliding down a rough ramp with friction coefficient $\mu > 0$.
misconceptions.repair: Kinetic friction is non-conservative ($W_f = -\mu mg \cos\theta \cdot d \neq 0$). The correct statement is $K_i + U_i + W_f = K_f + U_f \implies mgh - \mu mg \cos\theta \cdot d = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Assuming normal force work $W_N = 0$ in an accelerating elevator or on a movable wedge.
misconceptions.repair: $W = \int \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r}_{\text{point of contact}}$. If the contact surface itself moves along the normal vector (e.g. a rising elevator floor), $W_N = N \Delta y > 0$.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Calculating work done by tension in circular motion as $T \times 2\pi r$.
misconceptions.repair: At every instant, tension is perpendicular to instantaneous velocity ($\vec{T} \cdot \vec{v} = 0 \implies \vec{T} \cdot d\vec{r} = 0$). Therefore, work done by pure centripetal force is strictly zero.
